question: Given the rain of the whole local day t (00:00 to 24:00 by the local wall clock, from hourly ERA5) as one extra daily input, how many more onsets are warned 1 day ahead, and how much of the gap to the perfect weather forecast is closed - against the same rain one day older, against the rain table alone, and against NLDAS rain whose day ends in the evening?
outcome: Given the rain of the whole issue day up to local midnight (hourly ERA5 rain from 00:00 to 24:00 by the local wall clock) as one extra input to the LSTM with the river gauge, onsets warned 1 day ahead go from 19% to 29% (control 21%); the verdict is NOT YET.
outcome_caveat: The NLDAS rain up to the evening gives a higher share (30%, 183 hits of 611) than the rain to midnight (29%, 180 hits of 611); the five single trainings with the rain to midnight span 27.5% to 31.6%; the control is not flat (21% against 19% with the rain table alone); the success rule of the work order (clearly above the NLDAS result in every training, control flat) is not met. The control with the same rain over the table's own window is flat (20.3% against 18.7% with the rain table alone), so the gain of 9.2 points comes from the hours after about 09:00 (76 onsets warned only by the rain to midnight against 20 only by that control). Ridge regression and the random forest given the same input warn of 26.8% and 27.0% (the new input adds 16.2 and 8.8 points to them, 10.8 to the LSTM), so the gain does not need the network.
outcome_full: Given the rain of the whole issue day up to local midnight (hourly ERA5 rain from 00:00 to 24:00 by the local wall clock) as one extra input to the LSTM with the river gauge, onsets warned 1 day ahead go from 19% to 29% (control 21%); the verdict is NOT YET. The NLDAS rain up to the evening gives a higher share (30%, 183 hits of 611) than the rain to midnight (29%, 180 hits of 611); the five single trainings with the rain to midnight span 27.5% to 31.6%; the control is not flat (21% against 19% with the rain table alone); the success rule of the work order (clearly above the NLDAS result in every training, control flat) is not met. The control with the same rain over the table's own window is flat (20.3% against 18.7% with the rain table alone), so the gain of 9.2 points comes from the hours after about 09:00 (76 onsets warned only by the rain to midnight against 20 only by that control). Ridge regression and the random forest given the same input warn of 26.8% and 27.0% (the new input adds 16.2 and 8.8 points to them, 10.8 to the LSTM), so the gain does not need the network.

inputs.how_to_read: the hours each input covers, as the model reads them on issue day t. The forecast is issued at the end of day t, local midnight of the river-flow day

clock.input: prcp (Daymet rain, the rain table), srad, tmax, tmin, vp, dayl
clock.covers: for rain, a day that ends at about 09:00 local standard time on day t (basins 07:26 to 18:16; the four readings 07:28 to 10:42); the window of the other Daymet variables was not measured

clock.input: q_mm (observed river flow, with-gauge sets only)
clock.used_by: wq, wqn, wqh, wqf and their controls
clock.covers: the daily mean flow of local day t, midnight to midnight by the local clock, so the day ends at the issue time (in the 2012 check, while summer time was in force, by the summer clock at 10 of 12 gauges and by standard time at 2; by standard time in winter)

ERA5 hourly rain of the local wall-clock day t, summer time included: every hour goes to the local calendar day in which it ends, so the last hour of day t ends at 24:00 by the wall clock, the end of day t and the issue time; a day has 24 hours, or 23 or 25 where the clocks change; time zones: America/Chicago for Leaf River, MS (UTC-6 in winter); America/New_York for all other basins (UTC-5 in winter)
clock.source: data/hourly/era5_<gauge_id>.json, Open-Meteo archive API, ERA5, UTC, summed by this script

clock.covers: the same series one day older: on issue day t the model reads the rain of the local day t-1, from 00:00 to 24:00 of day t-1 by the wall clock
clock.source: the same series, one day later in the table

clock.covers: ERA5 hourly rain over the wall-clock window from 09:00 of day t-1 to 09:00 of day t, the window of the rain table itself (as measured in results/day_windows.json, day_ends.daymet: 08:48 local standard time, rounded to 09:00), summer time included: every hour goes to the window in which it ends; a window has 24 hours, or 23 or 25 where the clocks change; the last hour ends at 09:00 of day t, 15 hours before the issue time (local midnight at the end of day t); time zones: America/Chicago for Leaf River, MS (UTC-6 in winter); America/New_York for all other basins (UTC-5 in winter)

ERA5 hourly rain of the UTC day of the date of day t: from 00:00 UTC of that date to 00:00 UTC of the next date, always 24 hours (the day that a rain product served by UTC day holds, as IMERG at NASA POWER); in local standard time it ends at 19:00 in the Eastern basins and 18:00 in Central time, by the wall clock between 18:00 and 20:00 (summer time), 4 to 6 hours before the issue time (local midnight at the end of day t)
a day that ends at about 17:30 local standard time on day t (readings 16:40 to 19:28); if NLDAS is stamped by the UTC day, at 19:00 (18:00 in the Central-time basin)
clock.source: results/day_windows.json, day_ends.nldas; the column is built here as 10_rain_timing.py builds it (camels.load_basin(gauge_id, 'nldas'), prcp)

clock.input: the perfect forecast (the ladder; lstm_wf, lstm_wqf)
clock.covers: the Daymet weather stamped t+1, t+2 and t+3: an upper bound that cannot be had in practice
fixed numbers per basin, not daily data

questions_added_after_the_review: What are the hours 09:00 to 24:00 of day t worth, apart from having a second rain product? (wqh_to09: the same ERA5 hours over the window of the rain table)
What are the evening hours beyond the UTC day worth? (wqh_utc: the same ERA5 hours over the UTC day, what a rain product served by UTC day or IMERG-Early would hold at the issue time)
Do the NLDAS rain of the issue day and the rain to midnight together warn of more onsets than either? (wqnh)
Would ridge regression and a random forest gain from the new input as the LSTM does? (the yardstick, rule 2 of the work order)

control.what: the same ERA5 series one day older (on issue day t the model reads the rain of the local day t-1): a second rain product for the days up to t-1 that holds no rain later than the rain table. Test minus control is the worth of the rain of day t. Everything else (settings, seeds, inputs, training years) is equal.

matched_window_controls.what: added after the review of the first twelve trainings: the same ERA5 hours summed over the window of the rain table itself (wqh_to09: 09:00 of day t-1 to 09:00 of day t; a second rain product with no hour the table does not cover) and over the UTC day (wqh_utc: what a rain product served by UTC day, or IMERG-Early, would hold at the issue time). Test minus control is the worth of the hours 09:00 to 24:00 of day t, and of the evening hours beyond the UTC day.

validation_used_for_no_choice.label: USED FOR NO CHOICE. Validation years (2000-2005), shown for reference only: no input set, setting or stopping point of this script was chosen on these scores (the settings came from 04_lstm_all.py). value_of_hours_09_to_24.what: the worth of the hours 09:00 to 24:00 of day t, with the river gauge: lstm_wqh (ERA5 rain from 00:00 to 24:00 of day t) minus lstm_wqh_to09 (the same ERA5 hours over the window of the rain table itself, 09:00 of day t-1 to 09:00 of day t: a second rain product that holds no hour the table does not cover, as far as the table's window is known). The two differ only in the extra column; the same seed number gives the same starting weights and the same sequence of training samples (difference_by_seed). ITS COMPANION is second_rain_product_alone (lstm_wqh_to09 minus lstm_wq: 20.3% against 18.7%, +1.6 points, every seed above every seed: no): the control is flat, so this difference is the worth of the hours after about 09:00 and not that of having a second product. Quote the two together.

value_of_evening_hours_beyond_utc_day.what: the worth of the evening hours beyond the UTC day, with the river gauge: lstm_wqh (00:00 to 24:00 of day t) minus lstm_wqh_utc (the same ERA5 hours over the UTC day of day t, which ends at 00:00 UTC of day t+1, 19:00 local standard time in the Eastern basins and 18:00 in Leaf River): what a rain product served by UTC day, or IMERG-Early with its delay of about 4 hours, would hold at the issue time, so the difference is what the last hours before the issue time add to it (ERA5 stands in for such a product; it is not one). THIS IS A READING OF ERA5, whose rain is poorer than NLDAS's, and it is to be quoted together with nldas_rain_against_era5_over_the_utc_day: the NLDAS rain, whose day ends at about the hour at which the UTC day ends (17:30 as measured, 19:00 if it is stamped by the UTC day), reaches 30.0% (183 hits) against 29.5% (180 hits) for the ERA5 rain to midnight, while the ERA5 rain over the UTC day reaches 22.6% (138 hits). So the +6.9 points are what the evening hours beyond the UTC day add to ERA5, not what they add to any rain product.

value_of_hours_09_to_utc_day_end.what: the hours in between (an addition to the two readings asked for): lstm_wqh_utc minus lstm_wqh_to09, the worth of the hours from about 09:00 to the end of the UTC day (19:00 local standard time) of day t, so that the three controls read as a ladder: rain table window -> UTC day -> whole day.

second_rain_product_alone.what: what a second rain product with no new hours is worth: lstm_wqh_to09 minus lstm_wq (the rain table alone). If it is not above the seeds of lstm_wq the control is flat in the sense of the work order.

nldas_rain_against_era5_over_the_utc_day.what: an addition to the readings asked for: lstm_wqn (the NLDAS rain, whose day ends at about 17:30 local standard time as measured, at 19:00 if it is stamped by the UTC day) minus lstm_wqh_utc (the ERA5 rain over the UTC day, which ends at 19:00): two rain products over about the same window (NLDAS's day is known only to within the spread of the readings in results/day_windows.json), so the difference is mostly that of the product, a gauge-based analysis against a model reanalysis, and not that of the hours.

both_products.what: the NLDAS rain of the issue day and the rain to midnight (ERA5) together, with the river gauge: lstm_wqnh against lstm_wqh, against lstm_wqn and against lstm_wq. The NLDAS rung and the midnight rung warn of the same number of onsets but partly of different ones (overlap_of_warned_onsets), so this asks whether the two together warn of more.

by_period.how_to_read: onsets warned 1 day ahead (seed averages, pooled over the basins) and the median NSE, scored on the target days of the test years before and from 17 July 2009 (flood.evaluate with the test part cut in two). A description made after the fact, not one of the readings and not used for any choice: ERA5's rain was made without rain observations before that day and with radar and gauge rain assimilated over the USA from it, all training and validation years lie before it, and the two parts hold different numbers of onsets, so a difference between them is weak evidence unless it is large; onsets_warned_standard_error is sqrt(p(1-p)/n) of the share.

notes: Quoting. The sentence in `outcome` is accurate arithmetic but incomplete as a statement of the result: any document (report, README, slides, Q&A, guide) must quote `outcome_full` (the outcome plus `outcome_caveat`), never `outcome` alone. Both are computed from the tables of this file.

Clock of rain_to_midnight (the first new input; the windows added later follow in the note on the matched-window controls). The value of day t is the rain of the wall-clock day t at the gauge, summer time included (time zones: America/Chicago for Leaf River, MS (UTC-6 in winter); America/New_York for all other basins (UTC-5 in winter)). Every hourly value goes to the local calendar day in which its hour ENDS, and an hour that ends at exactly 24:00 belongs to the day that ends then. A day has 24 hours, or 23 or 25 where the clocks change: 34 days of 23 hours, 12350 of 24 and 34 of 25 (the same in every basin; daily_rain.day_lengths), and summer time is in force at the end of 58% of the days. The first hour of a day starts at 00:00 and the last ends at 24:00, the end of day t, when the forecast is issued. The code checks it for all 12 basins and all 12418 days (1980-10-01 to 2014-09-30, no gap, asserted): (1) every hour summed into a day starts at or after 00:00 and ends at or before 24:00 of that day, by the wall clock and in absolute (UTC) time; (2) the same daily rain by a second route, in which the UTC start and end of every day come from the time-zone rules (zoneinfo) and the hours between them are summed, and every hour lies in the same day as in the main route; (3) the rain of all hours after 24:00 of 3 random days per basin and of the first day of 23 and of 25 hours was replaced by made-up values: no value up to that day changed (daily_rain.clock).

Hour stamps. Open-Meteo documents its hourly precipitation as the 'sum of the preceding hour', so the value at time T is the rain of the hour that ENDS at T: the reading of check_day_windows.hourly(), copied here. ECMWF's own documentation of ERA5 says the same of the accumulations of the reanalysis (they are over the hour ending at the validity time; ECMWF Confluence, 'ERA5: data documentation', page read on 2026-10-07). The proofs of the clock in this file hold GIVEN that documented convention (the module header says so): it is documentation, not something this code or any test of the data proves. The data lean the same way but cannot prove it to the hour: the independent review (results/review_rain_to_midnight.json, check 3f, result 'supported, not proved') found that the correlation of the ERA5 stamps with the MERRA-2 hours (whose key is the START of the hour) peaks at a lag of -1 h (median of the basins), as 'hour ending at the stamp' predicts. Besides, in results/day_windows.json (calibration 2) IMERG, whose day is documented to be the UTC day, comes out 2.1 h late against ERA5 and 1.1 h late against MERRA-2, so the hourly references carry timing errors of about that size. If the values were instead the rain of the hour AFTER their stamp, each daily value would hold the first hour after midnight in place of the first hour of the day, and the saved networks would have read a series that differs by that hour: the independent review fed the networks of seeds 0-2 the series that results from the opposite convention (results/review_rain_to_midnight.json, check 3g; seeds 3-4 were not tested) and the share of onsets warned 1 day ahead moved by -0.7 points with the river gauge and -1.3 without it (median NSE -0.006 and -0.005): about one point, against a gain of 10.8 and 14.1 points that the new input brings.

Summer time. One rule for all basins: the day is the wall-clock day of the gauge, summer time included, not the standard-time day. Why: results/day_windows.json (15-minute flow of the gauges, 2012-03-13 to 2012-06-25, while summer time was in force) found that the daily flow of 10 of 12 gauges is a midnight-to-midnight mean by the summer clock (over the whole check, 2012-01-05 to 2012-06-25, standard-time weeks included, the tally is 7 by the summer clock and 5 by standard time), so their river-flow day, and with it the issue time of the forecast, ends at 24:00 by the wall clock, which is 23:00 standard time. For the other 2 gauges (Murder Creek, GA; Turkey Creek, GA) the flow day follows standard time, so the wall-clock day ends one hour before their flow day: for them one hour of rain is left out in summer, which can only lose information and never reads anything after the issue time. In winter the wall clock is standard time. Only 2012-01-05 to 2012-06-25 was checked, so how the flow days of the other years were cut is not known; the rule reads nothing after the issue time whether a gauge's flow day follows the wall clock or standard time. What the hour that is left out for some gauges in summer would be worth was not measured.

What the series is. ERA5 hourly rain is the output of short model forecasts (18 hours, run twice a day) started from the analyses of 06 and 18 UTC, as ECMWF's ERA5 documentation says (ECMWF Confluence, 'ERA5: data documentation', page read on 2026-10-07), not a gauge analysis: the hourly values are not corrected with rain gauges. E1 therefore measures what MODEL rain up to midnight is worth, a stand-in for radar or satellite rain: it is not rain that anyone could have read at midnight, and the title of E1 in the work order ('rain observed up to the issue time') is stronger than what was tested. Its timing within the day is also less sure than its daily total (the clock check above puts a number on that). In real time the same hours would come from radar and gauge analyses or from satellite rain such as IMERG-Early (a few hours late). The test shows what rain up to midnight is worth if it were known as well as ERA5 knows it, not what a real-time service delivers. One more fact bears on this: according to Beck et al. (2019, Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 23, 207, citing Lopez 2011 and 2013; read on 2026-10-07, not in ECMWF's own documentation page) the ERA5 analyses assimilate radar and gauge rain over the United States from 2009-07-17 on, so from then on the forecasts start from analyses that have seen observed rain and the ERA5 rain is probably closer to the truth. All training years (1980-2000) and all validation years lie before that date; 1902 of the 3287 test days (58%) lie after it. The series is therefore not of one quality in the training and the test years, and the worry is that this makes the later test years easier for every ERA5 input, the controls included. by_period shows what happens (a description made after the fact, not a test; the standard errors are sqrt(p(1-p)/n) of the shares): the rain to midnight warns of 27.5% of the 200 onsets before the change (standard error 3.2 points) and of 30.4% of the 411 onsets after it (2.3 points), and its gain over the rain table alone is +13.0 points before and +9.7 after, so the gain is not smaller before the change than after it: the worry is not borne out.

One grid cell, not a basin mean. The series is the value of the ERA5 grid point that the service returned for the basin centroid (on a regular 0.25 degree grid, up to 0.12 degrees from the centroid; daily_rain.clock holds each point). The Daymet rain of the table is a basin average. Over the whole record the ERA5 daily rain is 0.85 times the Daymet rain in the median basin (daily_rain.check). A storm can reach the cell and the basin at different hours. The 12 basins are served by 11 distinct ERA5 grid cells: Catawba, NC and South Toe, NC share the one cell at 35.75, -82.25 and so get the identical series (daily_rain.grid.cells).

Day alignment. The Daymet rain stamped day d correlates 0.53 with the ERA5 rain of the local day d, 0.56 with that of day d-1 and 0.05 with that of day d+1 (median of the 12 basins; daily_rain.check). A Daymet day that ends in the morning (09:00 local time, readings 07:28 to 10:42) shares its hours with two local days, d-1 and d, and none with d+1: the correlations show that pattern, so the two series are aligned as described.

Control: the same series one day older (on issue day t the model reads the ERA5 rain of the local day t-1, from 00:00 to 24:00 of that day by the wall clock). The Daymet value of day t reaches to about 09:00 on day t, so the table holds the hours of the control, the later ones under day t and the earlier ones under day t-1. The control therefore adds a second rain product for the days up to t-1 and no rain the table does not already hold; test minus control is the worth of the ERA5 rain of day t. That is mostly rain after about 09:00, which the table does not hold yet, but also a second estimate of the rain of the night before, which the Daymet value of day t already covers; this control alone cannot separate the two, and the matched-window control wqh_to09 (note on the matched-window controls) does. The first day of the control keeps its own value (as in 10_rain_timing.py); it is read only in the warm-up of a training sequence and never scored.

Ladder (ladder, closure). The rungs are the rain table alone (Daymet; its day ends at about 09:00), NLDAS rain (its day ends at about 17:30 on the readings of day_windows.json, 16:40 to 19:28; stamped by the UTC day it would end at 19:00, 18:00 in the Central-time basin), the rain of the whole day to 24:00, the NLDAS rain and the rain of the whole day together (wqnh), and the perfect weather forecast, an upper bound that cannot be had in practice. The sets of the rain-table, NLDAS and perfect-forecast rungs and the NLDAS controls are read from the prediction files of 04_lstm_all.py and 10_rain_timing.py, not trained again. All sets are compared on identical days (coverage 1.0 for every model, lead and basin, asserted for the test and the validation years). The share closed is not the whole time-stamp part of the gap: the perfect-forecast sets read the Daymet weather stamped t+1 to t+3, which also holds rain still to come, and ERA5 and Daymet are different products, so the split is approximate.

Same settings and seeds as 04_lstm_all.py (results/lstm_all.json, key config): the trainings differ from its models only in the extra input column (two columns for wqnh), so a difference to lstm_wq / lstm_w is the effect of that column (and of the training noise the seed range shows). The three sets added after the review (wqh_to09, wqh_utc, wqnh) were trained with the settings stored in the results file of the first run, which are those of results/lstm_all.json (asserted when they were made), and with the same seeds (0-2 then; seeds 3 and 4 were added to all seven sets alike on 30 October 2026). For two sets with the same number of inputs the same seed gives the same starting weights and the same training samples, so the seed-by-seed differences in value_of_hours_09_to_24 and value_of_evening_hours_beyond_utc_day compare two trainings that start alike and differ in the extra column (the later steps differ, because the data do); wqnh has one input more, so its starting weights differ.

The checks (gain_rule). A gain in the median NSE is called clear when three things agree: every single seed with the new input is above every single seed of the model it is compared with (the comparison is made with the control, with the rain table alone, and with the NLDAS rain); the NSE is higher in most of the 12 basins; and the Wilcoxon signed-rank p (two-sided, over the basins) is below 0.05. The onsets warned are pooled over the basins, so no basin count or p exists for them: there only the seeds are compared (as in 10_rain_timing.py). The basins share storms, so p describes and does not prove; 10_rain_timing.py stored no p, and the one here is added with the test of 04_lstm_all.py. With one seed (a smoke test) no seed range can say anything.

Clock of the matched-window controls (rain_to_09 and rain_utc_day). The same hourly ERA5 values as rain_to_midnight, summed over other windows by the same code, and proved for all 12 basins and all 12418 days in the same way: (1) every hour summed into day t starts at or after the start and ends at or before the end of its window, in absolute (UTC) time and on the clock of the window, and ends at or before the issue time of day t (local midnight at the end of day t, as a UTC time, and 24:00 by the wall clock); (2) the same daily rain by a second route, from the time-zone rules, and every hour lies in the same day in both routes; (3) the rain after the end of the window of 3 random days per basin, and of the first days of 23 and of 25 hours, was replaced by made-up values: no value up to that day changed (daily_rain.windows). The code for any window reproduces rain_to_midnight exactly (asserted). rain_to_09 is the wall-clock window from 09:00 of day t-1 to 09:00 of day t, the window of the rain table itself: results/day_windows.json (day_ends.daymet) measured it to end at 08:48 local standard time (basins 07:26 to 18:16, readings 07:28 to 10:42), rounded to 09:00; the code uses the wall clock like the main series, so in summer it ends one hour earlier in standard time, well inside the spread of the readings. Its last hour ends 15 hours before the issue time. rain_utc_day is the UTC day of the date of day t: from 00:00 UTC of that date to 00:00 UTC of the next date, always 24 hours, 19:00 local standard time in the Eastern basins and 18:00 in Leaf River, by the wall clock between 18:00 and 20:00; its last hour ends 4 to 6 hours before the issue time, so the proof of nothing after the issue time holds with that margin. A rain product served by UTC day (IMERG at NASA POWER) or IMERG-Early with its delay of about 4 hours would have that UTC day at about the issue time; ERA5 summed over the UTC day stands in for it and is not it.

What the two controls are for. Test minus control is the worth of what the test series holds and the control does not. rain_to_09 is a second ERA5 product over the window of the table (as nearly as that window is known: it differs from basin to basin and between the readings), so it holds no hour that the table does not already cover, give or take the uncertainty of that window, and lstm_wqh minus lstm_wqh_to09 is the worth of the hours 09:00 to 24:00 of day t (value_of_hours_09_to_24), without the effect of having a second product; the Daymet rain stamped d correlates 0.75 with rain_to_09 of the same day, against 0.53 with rain_to_midnight (median of the basins; daily_rain.check_windows). rain_utc_day holds the hours up to the end of the UTC day, so lstm_wqh minus lstm_wqh_utc is the worth of the evening hours beyond it (value_of_evening_hours_beyond_utc_day). The NLDAS day, as measured, is about 17:30 local standard time and, if stamped by the UTC day, 19:00; the NLDAS rain of the CAMELS files correlates 0.76 with rain_utc_day of the same day, 0.72 with rain_to_midnight and 0.54 with rain_to_09 (the ERA5 window that NLDAS resembles most: rain_utc_day).

The NLDAS column of wqnh. prcp_nldas is the 'prcp' column of the nldas forcing files that camels.load_basin(gauge_id, 'nldas') reads, over the same days as the Daymet table, built by the same expression as the column of the wn / wqn sets of 10_rain_timing.py, with the same two asserts (the same days as the Daymet table, no gaps). Its clock is not proved again here; this file relies on the reading of 10_rain_timing.py and of results/day_windows.json: NLDAS rain of day d correlates 0.80 with IMERG of the same UTC day, 0.24 with the UTC day before and 0.11 with the one after (results/rain_timing.json, notes), so the NLDAS day is the UTC day or ends a little earlier, not later; the day ends at about 17:30 local standard time on the readings of results/day_windows.json (16:40 to 19:28), hours before the issue time, so its day stamp leaks nothing. In wqnh it comes together with rain_to_midnight, whose clock is proved above; both end before the issue time.

Check of this script's own scoring code against the stored numbers of the earlier scripts (checks_against_stored_results): 42 of 42 numbers of 10_rain_timing.py (median NSE and onsets warned of the rungs) and 108 of 108 verdict numbers of 06_flood_analysis.py agree.

This file was written by --rescore: every score, table and note and the figure were recomputed from the saved prediction sets lstm_<set>_s<seed> (and base_linreg_wqh, base_rf_wqh) without training again; the training records in models.<set>.per_seed, training, n_trainings, training_seconds and runtime_s are those of the training runs; the reload check was run again on the saved networks unless reload_check says it was carried over. rescore_runtime_s is the time of this pass. passes lists the training passes and, last, this rescore, each with the sha256 of the script that ran it; the earlier passes were made by versions of the script that no longer exist, so their hash is 'not recorded' and not guessed.
runtime_s leaves out the time the script waited for the CPU (waited_for_cpu_s); training_seconds is the time of the trainings alone.

101 values in this file are not numbers (NaN: shares whose denominator is zero, for example the share of false warnings of a model that gave no warning, or a p-value that is not defined); they are written as null (strict JSON; several other results files of this project still hold bare NaN tokens). A reader must treat null as 'no value'.

The reviews were written by an AI agent, not by a team member: the team's own check (team.json) is still open.

The ranges of code/13_uncertainty.py (test years and basins drawn again) are still not extended to the new prediction sets (lstm_wqh, lstm_wqh_older, lstm_wh, lstm_wh_older, lstm_wqh_to09, lstm_wqh_utc, lstm_wqnh, base_linreg_wqh, base_rf_wqh); the seed ranges and the checks of gain_rule are all this file holds.

The matched-window controls and the combined set were run with the river gauge only: wh_to09, wh_utc and wnh do not exist, so what the extra hours and the two rain products are worth to the model WITHOUT the river gauge, where the rain should matter more, is not known.

More seeds where the NSE decides: the median NSE of the single trainings of a set spans up to 0.164 (lead 1, lstm_wqh_to09: 0.416 to 0.580), while the validation NSE of the same trainings spans only 0.378 to 0.388, so the validation years cannot tell a good training from a weak one. With five seeds the NSE rule of report section 4.2 (every single seed above every single seed, higher in most basins, p below 0.05) can hardly ever call a gain of this size clear: value_of_hours_09_to_24 is +0.124 in NSE, higher in 12 of 12 basins (p < 0.001), and the rule reads it as 'no clear difference'. The onsets warned, pooled over the basins, are decided by the seeds more easily.

No other windows than the three tried (the whole day, the window of the rain table, the UTC day) and no other hours (for example rain up to the early evening in steps, to see how the gain grows with the hours); no basin mean of the rain (one grid cell per basin, 11 cells for 12 basins); no other rain product (IMERG-Early, radar, AORC) and no second reanalysis for the hours; the UTC-day control is ERA5 summed over the UTC day, not IMERG.

For the gauges whose flow day follows standard time in summer (results/day_windows.json), the wall-clock day ends one hour before their flow day, so one hour of rain is left out of the new input for them in summer; what that hour would add was not measured, and the flow-day check covers only part of one year.

The settings of the LSTM (hidden size, learning rate, dropout, budget) were not tuned again for the new inputs: they are those chosen by 04_lstm_all.py for the other input sets. The simple models use the settings chosen by 02_baselines.py for wq; each was fitted once (the forest has one random seed), so no seed range exists for them.
No leave-one-basin-out test, no lead other than 1 to 3 days, no peaks-and-onsets loss (E5), no change of the network (E6).

The ladder sets (lstm_w, lstm_wq, lstm_wf, lstm_wqf, lstm_wn, lstm_wqn and the NLDAS controls) were not trained again; they were scored here with the same code as the new sets. Their networks were never saved, so only the sets of this script can forecast again without training.

Problem P2 of NEXT_STEPS_FOR_AGENTS.md also asks for a script that loads the saved networks and forecasts a new day or river; none was written. reload_check shows that the files are enough to forecast again on the tables of this project.

The report subsection and the rung of the key figure for E1 (NEXT_STEPS_FOR_AGENTS.md, section 6), and the update of PLAN.md and README.md, are not made: documents must quote outcome_full, not outcome alone.

ERA5's rain changes on 17 July 2009, when radar and gauge rain begin to be assimilated over the United States (a literature fact, Beck et al. 2019; not found in ECMWF's own documentation page): the models were trained on years before that day and 58% of the test days lie after it. by_period only describes the two parts of the test years; no rain product of constant quality (AORC, Stage IV: ROADMAP.md, step 1b) was tried, and the models were not retrained on the years after the change.
